title: Weekly Briefing: Accenture's $29 AI Limit, McKinsey's New AI Interview, and Bank of America's 1,000-Person AI Security Push
author: Jacob Morgan
summary: Jacob Morgan's Future Ready Leadership Weekly Briefing looks at three stories showing the second-order effects of AI inside large organizations. The first is Accenture's cap on centrally funded Claude spending at $29 per employee per month, which Morgan reads as AI usage becoming a real operating expense that needs an owner and as a sign that AI access is becoming part of job design. The second is McKinsey's pilot of a 10-minute interview with an AI-generated client, which he finds more interesting than AI résumé screening because it tests real-time judgment that candidates cannot rehearse. The third is Bank of America adding 1,000 contractors to patch software vulnerabilities surfaced by advanced AI models, which shows that AI can create new work even as it saves money. Each item is paired with Morgan's own commentary on what it means for leaders, HR, and hiring.
points: Accenture's $29 allowance suggests different roles will need different levels of AI spend, so giving everyone the same tool and budget may make as little sense as giving everyone the same software stack.
Morgan argues the next phase of enterprise AI is disciplined spending that asks which use cases deserve $30, $300, or $1,000 a month.
McKinsey's AI client interview tests unpredictable real-time thinking, which may make hiring more human because the hardest skills to fake are human ones.
Bank of America's contractor surge shows AI can find problems faster than people can fix them, so productivity gains create bottlenecks elsewhere.
The briefing's common thread is that the real question is where the work moves after AI changes the system, not whether AI saves labor.
quotes: What it does show is that AI usage is becoming a real operating expense that somebody eventually has to own.
Which use cases deserve $30 a month? Which deserve $300? Which deserve $1,000 because they are producing enough value to justify it?
AI access is quickly becoming part of job design. Different roles may require very different levels of AI capability and spend.
Traditional interviews reward preparation. Candidates rehearse common questions, memorize frameworks, and increasingly use AI to prepare polished responses.
The irony is that AI may end up making hiring more human because the skills that become hardest to fake are increasingly human ones.
AI can save enormous amounts of money while simultaneously creating entirely new categories of work and expense.
The technology found problems faster than humans could fix them, so the company needed more humans.
The real question is not simply whether AI saves labor. It is where the work moves after AI changes the system.
